description: Project Mercury Team is a community of developers, innovators, and space enthusiasts turning complex NASA challenges into accessible solutions. Our project, SKYSHIFT, makes SPHEREx data easier to explore through interactive 3D visualization and intuitive tools. We bring skills in software engineering, research, and design, and welcome teammates in astronomy, AI, data science, UI/UX, and 3D development. Join us to build technology that brings space science closer to everyone!
summary:
SKYSHIFT is a public web tool for exploring real NASA SPHEREx infrared observations of any patch of sky over time. Enter right ascension and declination, or choose one of the five challenge targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), and SKYSHIFT retrieves dated SPHEREx cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA and shows them as a flipbook. Users can blink through exposures, compare two dates side by side, with a wipe, or as a difference, and use the Same band control to limit playback to frames at a similar wavelength. Each frame shows its date, detector, wavelength, quality flags and a link to the original archive product, and Gaia and AllWISE overlays are available for context.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is far too much data for any one person or program to sift through. SKYSHIFT helps students and citizen scientists see how a field changes and decide what deserves a closer look. It claims no discoveries.
details:
What it does and how it works
SKYSHIFT is a web viewer for NASA SPHEREx infrared observations. A visitor chooses one of the five challenge targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or enters right ascension and declination, then picks a field width and data release. SKYSHIFT shows dated cutouts from DR1 and QR3 and lets users blink through them, or compare two frames side by side, with a wipe, or as a difference. The Same band control limits playback to frames from one detector at similar wavelengths, so changes in colour are less likely to be mistaken for changes in the sky. Each frame shows its date, detector, wavelength, quality flags and a link to the original archive product. Users can also choose coadds per detector, sample a spectrum from the loaded frames, and add Gaia DR3 and AllWISE markers or a DSS background. Shared links keep the coordinates, field width and comparison settings, so views can be embedded or passed on.

Benefits and intended impact
SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is too much for any one person to inspect. SKYSHIFT gives students and citizen scientists a simple way to look at the same patch of sky across dates and decide what deserves a closer look. It claims no detections.

Tools and technology
A Python service queries NASA/IPAC IRSA and prepares real cutouts with Astropy (FITS, time, WCS and wavelength handling), NumPy, SciPy and reproject. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Canvas, with a locally bundled CDS Aladin Lite for the DSS background and Three.js for an optional illustrative spacecraft model. We run it in Docker on Render and tested it with Playwright and axe. Targets get catalogue positions and proper motions from SIMBAD. Each preset cutout is centred on the object’s position at the time of that exposure. Five bundled previews open instantly; other searches go live to IRSA.

Creativity and design factors
We built a flipbook that stays honest about its data. It shows masked pixels instead of hiding them, labels every display aid (such as gap fill) as cosmetic, and warns when frames differ in wavelength or release. We also considered accessibility (keyboard controls, reduced motion, screen-reader labels), mobile use, and how fast new data releases can be added.

Limitations
SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcseconds wide, so even fast-moving targets such as Barnard’s Star and WISE 0855 shift only about 1–2 pixels in a year. The bundled previews cover a subset of observations, and live searches depend on IRSA being available. Bright stars can saturate and mask the target pixel.

Project history and AI assistance
The team adapted an existing SKYSHIFT application for this challenge. The README’s Project history section documents the earlier work and the changes made during the event. OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude assisted as disclosed in the Use of SI field and in the repository. Source: https://github.com/MuathYasin000/SKYSHIFT-
